Pool pumps, crop irrigation, and Level 1 EVs tend to require 6-10 hours of demand per day, so some of their load also appears in the very early morning hours; Level 2 EVs, on the other hand, can complete all of their required charging in the middle of the day. It is notable that, on the average day, zero EV or pool pumping occurs after 4pm, and only a marginal amount of crop irrigation. Space cooling also shows a sharp increase in daytime loads, though these loads occur a bit earlier in the morning than perhaps expected. Firstly, it is notable that the baseline space conditioning load shapes in the Res and Com sector are nearly identical; this is due to the use of a temperature regression model to develop these load shapes. Typically, it is expected that residential cooling loads occur later in the evening, as people are out of the home during the day. While the regression model did set different parameters for different blocks of the day, the underlying data did not send strong enough signals for those parameters to differ over time between the two sectors. Future work should explore the current understanding of the timing of space cooling loads, and how that has changed with recent remote work trends. For now, this 27 analysis assumes that the baseline cooling and heating loads are tied directly to outdoor temperature. Cooling loads are reduced throughout the afternoon and evening, with load primarily shifted to the late morning, when prices are lowest. It should be noted that this type of response may not be feasible for buildings that have poor insulation; precooling in the late morning and continuing to cool throughout early afternoon (at a lower level) may not allow for evening load reductions to occur. Finally, the space and water heating end uses exhibit similar patterns of load shifting with two shifts occurring each day in the morning and afternoon. Figure 13. Average daily end use load response, relative to baseline demand, for nine end use- sector combinations modeled in the study. 28 Figure 14 shows the aggregate load impact for all end uses modeled on the average day and the day with the peak system net load. EVs have the largest consistent year-round impact, increasing daytime loads over 5 GW on average and shedding approximately 1.5 GW of load in all hours of the evening. Space cooling adds an additional 5.8 GW at noon on the average day and sheds an average of another 2 GW in the late afternoon and early evening. Pool pumps and water heating have a consistent impact as well. On the peak net load day, the end use load response is noticeably different. Firstly, while EV load is reduced in the evening, it is not increased in the day.
